Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings:
A Constructive and Elementary Proof of ω≤9/4\omega\leq 9/4

Rafael Pass ††thanks: Pearl Research, Cornell Tech, Technion, TAU
Abstract

We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies ω≤9/4\omega\leq 9/4. This bound was recently claimed by OpenAI [Ope26a] through non-constructive arguments in Strassen’s asymptotic spectral framework, counting exact scalar arithmetic operations over the complex numbers. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every γ>0\gamma>0, the resulting algorithm multiplies two n×nn\times n integer matrices using O⁡(n9/4+γ)O(n^{9/4+\gamma}) integer arithmetic operations.

1 Introduction

The exponent ω\omega of matrix multiplication is the infimum of all τ\tau such that two n×nn\times n matrices can be multiplied with O⁡(nτ)O(n^{\tau}) arithmetic operations. Strassen [Str69] showed ω≤log2⁡7<2.81\omega\leq\log_{2}7<2.81. Later bounds follow a scheme developed by Bini, Capovani, Romani, and Lotti [BCRL79, Bin80], Schönhage [Sch81], and Strassen [Str87]. An explicit identity computes several products together, possibly with an error that vanishes with a parameter. Combining identities amplifies the saving, and the resulting independent products give a bound on ω\omega. Refinements of Strassen’s laser method, starting from the identity of Coppersmith and Winograd [CW90], reached ω<2.371339\omega<2.371339 [ADV+25] and ω<2.371177\omega<2.371177 [DEK+26].

OpenAI recently claimed ω≤9/4\omega\leq 9/4 [Ope26a], following a companion bound ω<2.258\omega<2.258 [Ope26b], starting from identities for polynomial multiplication. Their theorem is stated for exact arithmetic over the complex numbers, charging unit cost per scalar operation. Their proof uses Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum [Str88], an algebraic and topological framework for comparing bilinear maps through numerical invariants. Concavity strengthens inequalities for these invariants; spectral duality then converts them into the exponent bound. Their argument establishes the exponent bound without explicitly constructing the corresponding algorithms.

We give an explicit, constructive algorithm reaching the same bound using integer arithmetic throughout; furthermore, our construction is self-contained. Our starting point is the three-for-one polynomial degeneration of [Ope26a, Lemma 4.2]. We generalize it to a (c+2)(c+2)-for-cc polynomial packing and nexy use our (c+2)(c+2)-for-cc gadget, together with tensoring, to construct a Strassen-style identity: a fixed v×vv\times v block matrix product can be computed using rr products of linear combinations of its blocks, with logv⁡r\log_{v}r arbitrarily close to 9/49/4. This replaces the usual v3v^{3} block products by rr, just as Strassen replaces eight by seven. Applying the fixed identity recursively then gives the exponent bound.

Theorem 1.1.

For every γ>0\gamma>0, there is an explicit recursive algorithm that, for every positive integer nn, multiplies two n×nn\times n integer matrices with O⁡(n9/4+γ)O(n^{9/4+\gamma}) integer arithmetic operations. In particular, ω≤9/4\omega\leq 9/4.

The algorithm remains “galactic”: the constants hidden in the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) notation are enormous.

1.1 Our techniques

We first introduce the notion of a polynomial packing (PP): a procedure that recovers a collection of polynomial-product coefficients through linear encodings, source polynomial products, and linear decoding. Its efficiency depends on both the number and the dimensions of the source products.

Polynomial packing.

We now construct a (c+2)(c+2)-for-cc packing modulo ε\varepsilon, generalizing the three-for-one construction of [Ope26a, Lemma 4.2]. Consider univariate polynomials A,P1,…,Pc+1A,P_{1},\ldots,P_{c+1} with matrix coefficients, where AA has length aa and each PiP_{i} has length bb. Write [zk]​H[z^{k}]H for the coefficient matrix of zkz^{k} in HH, taking coefficients outside its range to be zero. We want to compute all coefficients of the c+1c+1 products A​P1,…,A​Pc+1AP_{1},\ldots,AP_{c+1}, which we call full products. Naively, this takes c+1c+1 polynomial multiplications. Introduce a polynomial QQ of length a+b−1a+b-1 and write Q=∑j=0c−1qj​zjQ=\sum_{j=0}^{c-1}q_{j}z^{j}, padding with zeros. Let ε\varepsilon be a formal parameter.

Modify the encoding to

Ej=Pj−z​Pj+1+ε​zb​qj−1,1≤j≤c.E_{j}=P_{j}-zP_{j+1}+\varepsilon z^{b}q_{j-1},\qquad 1\leq j\leq c.

∑j=1czj−1​A​Ej=A​P1−zc​A​Pc+1+ε​zb​A​Q.\sum_{j=1}^{c}z^{j-1}AE_{j}=AP_{1}-z^{c}AP_{c+1}+\varepsilon z^{b}AQ.

Dividing them by ε\varepsilon recovers these coefficients of A​QAQ exactly; we call this output a middle product. (A​Pi)i=1c+1⏟c+1​ full products([zk]​(A​Q))k=a−1a+b−2⏟1​ middle product(modε).\underbrace{(AP_{i})_{i=1}^{c+1}}_{c+1\text{ full products}}\qquad\underbrace{\bigl([z^{k}](AQ)\bigr)_{k=a-1}^{a+b-2}}_{1\text{ middle product}}\qquad\pmod{\varepsilon}.

To see the gain and its cost, take a=b=La=b=L and c=3​Lc=3L. The encoded polynomials then have length L+1=(1+3/c)​LL+1=(1+3/c)L. The additional middle window increases the number of outputs from c+1c+1 to c+2c+2 without increasing the source lengths. The balanced primal/dual construction below converts this improvement into an exponent saving.

We also construct and rely on a dual of the above packing, which reverses the roles: it computes c+1c+1 middle products and one full product modulo ε\varepsilon using cc slightly longer middle-product calls. We obtain it by exchanging and transposing the linear encoding and decoding maps. Transposition preserves the constant coefficient of the decoded map.

Amplifying the gain: Multivariate Packing.

Running the primal and dual packings side by side gives c+2c+2 full and c+2c+2 middle outputs from cc full and cc middle source products. Their counts add, so the gain remains 2​(c+2)/(2​c)=(c+2)/c2(c+2)/(2c)=(c+2)/c. To multiply the gain, we move to multivariate polynomials and apply the packings in separate variables. In two variables x,yx,y, one primal step in xx and one dual step in yy give (c+2)2(c+2)^{2} outputs from c2c^{2} source products; continuing in additional variables multiplies the gain further. To see why, start with one common left polynomial A⁡(x,y)A(x,y) of length aa in each variable and a (c+2)×(c+2)(c+2)\times(c+2) table of independent right polynomials Bi,j​(x,y)B_{i,j}(x,y). We want coefficients of each product A​Bi,jAB_{i,j}. For rows 1,…,c+11,\ldots,c+1, we want Full in xx; for the last row, Mid in xx. For columns 1,…,c+11,\ldots,c+1, we want Mid in yy; for the last column, Full in yy. Each Bi,jB_{i,j} has length bb in a variable where we want Full and length a+b−1a+b-1 where we want Mid. Figure 2 shows every row and column for c=4c=4.

For example, each of the (c+1)2(c+1)^{2} upper-left products requests [xk​yℓ]​(A​Bi,j)[x^{k}y^{\ell}](AB_{i,j}) for 0≤k<a+b−10\leq k<a+b-1 and a−1≤ℓ<a+b−1a-1\leq\ell<a+b-1; its right input has lengths (b,a+b−1)(b,a+b-1). Every column supplies the c+1c+1 full-range inputs and one middle-range input needed by the primal packing in xx. Every row supplies the c+1c+1 middle-range inputs and one full-range input needed by the dual packing in yy.

As above, take c≥a+2​b−1c\geq a+2b-1. In each column, apply the primal encoder in xx, viewing the coefficients as polynomials in yy. This leaves cc rows, with the yy-lengths unchanged. In each resulting row, apply the dual encoder in yy, viewing the coefficients as polynomials in xx. We now have a c×cc\times c table of encoded right polynomials, each of length b+1b+1 in xx and a+ba+b in yy. Multiply each by AA, computing all xx-coefficients and the yy-coefficients at exponents a−1,…,a+b−1a-1,\ldots,a+b-1. Apply the dual decoder in yy, then the primal decoder in xx.

Encoding in xx and then in yy, computing the source products, and decoding in reverse order recovers all the requested outputs modulo ε\varepsilon. This follows by applying the correctness of the two univariate packings along their separate coefficient indices.

We therefore recover (c+2)2(c+2)^{2} outputs from c2c^{2} source products. Furthermore, continuing this process in additional variables amplifies the compression exponentially. Use 2​d2d variables z1,…,z2​dz_{1},\ldots,z_{2d}, applying the primal packing in the first dd and the dual packing in the last dd. Encode in each variable, compute the resulting products, and decode in reverse order. This gives (c+2)2​d(c+2)^{2d} outputs from c2​dc^{2d} source products, a compression factor of ((c+2)/c)2​d((c+2)/c)^{2d}.

There is one issue: the source products are all Full in the first dd variables and Mid in the last dd, whereas the recovered outputs can have different numbers of Full and Mid directions. To obtain a recursive rule that we can apply repeatedly, we need to “end where we started”: the targets must have the same form as the sources. This requires, in particular, dd Full and dd Mid directions in each target, so we keep only these outputs. For example, in the two-variable table, the yellow and green outputs have two Full or two Mid directions, respectively, so they do not qualify. The (c+1)2(c+1)^{2} blue outputs and the single purple output have one of each: 2626 of the 3636 outputs when c=4c=4. With 2​d2d variables, we recover at least

(c+2)2​dd+1\frac{(c+2)^{2d}}{d+1}

outputs of this shape.11 1 To see why, consider the following equivalent counting question. Form a word whose first dd letters are chosen from {𝖥1,…,𝖥c+1,𝖬}\{\mathsf{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{F}_{c+1},\mathsf{M}\} and whose last dd letters are chosen from {𝖥,𝖬1,…,𝖬c+1}\{\mathsf{F},\mathsf{M}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{M}_{c+1}\}. All 𝖥\mathsf{F}-letters have type Full and all 𝖬\mathsf{M}-letters have type Mid; subscripts distinguish different letters of the same type. How many words contain exactly dd letters of each type? The answer is ∑h=0d(dh)2​(c+1)2​(d−h)\sum_{h=0}^{d}\binom{d}{h}^{2}(c+1)^{2(d-h)}, which is at least (c+2)2​d/(d+1)(c+2)^{2d}/(d+1) by Cauchy–Schwarz and the binomial theorem. Thus requiring this common shape costs at most a factor d+1d+1 in the output count, while the compression gain grows exponentially in dd. (Their Full and Mid directions may occupy different positions; the next step lets us align each target with the sources, which are Full in the first dd variables and Mid in the last dd.)

From SL-PP to PP.

So far, the same-left polynomial packing (SL-PP) computes ww retained targets sharing one left input AA. We now want independent pairs Ai,BiA_{i},B_{i}. Write each right input as

Bi=[Bi,0⋯Bi,w−1],B_{i}=[\,B_{i,0}\ \cdots\ B_{i,w-1}\,],

where the brackets denote horizontal concatenation of column blocks in every coefficient matrix. Thus group ii consists of the blocks of one BiB_{i}, all multiplied by the same AiA_{i}. We batch the AiA_{i} into one auxiliary univariate polynomial A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) satisfying A⁡(i)=AiA(i)=A_{i}. For each ii, encode the column blocks Bi,jB_{i,j} in a univariate polynomial Bi′​(ξ)B_{i}^{\prime}(\xi) satisfying Bi′​(i+ε​j)=Bi,jB_{i}^{\prime}(i+\varepsilon j)=B_{i,j}. Both encodings have degree at most w−1w-1, so the requested coefficients of A⁡(ξ)​Bi′​(ξ)A(\xi)B_{i}^{\prime}(\xi) are polynomials of degree at most 2​w−22w-2 in ξ\xi. We recover these polynomials by interpolation from 2​w−12w-1 common evaluation points. Fix one such point kk. We need the requested coefficients of the products A⁡(k)​B0′​(k),…,A⁡(k)​Bw−1′​(k)A(k)B_{0}^{\prime}(k),\ldots,A(k)B_{w-1}^{\prime}(k). Their right inputs differ, but their left input is the single value A⁡(k)A(k) of the polynomial encoding all the AiA_{i}. Thus one application of the same-left packing computes all these products’ requested coefficients modulo ε\varepsilon. We repeat this for each of the 2​w−12w-1 evaluation points; A⁡(k)A(k) may change between applications. Evaluating the recovered polynomials at i+ε​ji+\varepsilon j gives the requested coefficients of Ai​Bi,jA_{i}B_{i,j} modulo ε\varepsilon, since A⁡(i+ε​j)≡Ai(modε)A(i+\varepsilon j)\equiv A_{i}\pmod{\varepsilon}.22 2 The formal proof replaces the original packing’s parameter by εw\varepsilon^{w}, ensuring that divisions by ε\varepsilon in the right-input encoding leave the decoded error divisible by ε\varepsilon. Concatenating these output blocks recovers the requested coefficients of Ai​BiA_{i}B_{i} for each ii. (OpenAI [Ope26a] proves a related separation lemma using finite Fourier projection and a weight degeneration.)

A Strassen-like identity.

Transposing the matrix products gives a row-reduction gadget. Exchanging the left-input and output roles, by transposing the corresponding encoding and decoding maps, gives an inner-dimension reduction. Combining these with the column reduction gives one gadget that reduces all three matrix dimensions simultaneously. The resulting family is ordinary matrix multiplication at a=b=1a=b=1, is symmetric in a,ba,b under fixed coefficient permutations, and at a=b=La=b=L can be computed using O⁡(L6​d)O(L^{6d}) matrix multiplications. We can therefore compose a step increasing bb with one increasing aa: for d=c3d=c^{3}, one round increases both lengths by a factor approaching 1+3/c1+3/c, reduces each matrix dimension by approximately (1+2/c)4​d(1+2/c)^{4d}, and multiplies the number of remaining products by at most 6464. The exponent approaches

log⁡64+6​d​log⁡(1+3/c)4​d​log⁡(1+2/c)⟶94.\frac{\log 64+6d\log(1+3/c)}{4d\log(1+2/c)}\longrightarrow\frac{9}{4}.

After finitely many rounds, amplification and constant-coefficient interpolation give a fixed exact rational identity with this saving. Clearing its denominators and applying ordinary block recursion gives our integer-arithmetic algorithm.

2 Polynomial packings

We now define packing and the two operations used to build larger packings. We then construct the univariate gadgets, combine them across variables, and give their targets independent left inputs. We first fix notation for polynomials, linear maps, and their matrix inputs.

All vector spaces and linear maps are over ℚ\mathbb{Q} unless a formal parameter is displayed. A polynomial has length aa in a variable if its degree in that variable is less than aa; for several variables, the bounds apply separately. We identify a polynomial with its coefficient list, write [𝐳𝝂]​A[\mathbf{z}^{\boldsymbol{\nu}}]A for a coefficient, and set coefficients outside the specified bounds to zero. Input coefficient sizes p×q,q×rp\times q,q\times r mean that each coefficient of AA is a p×qp\times q matrix and each coefficient of BB is a q×rq\times r matrix.

For lists, a linear map has the form E​(U)k=∑iek​i​UiE(U)_{k}=\sum_{i}e_{ki}U_{i}; we use E⁡(U)E(U) and E​UEU interchangeably. The bilinear maps used for polynomial products have the form

F​(A,B)k=∑i,jfi​j​k​Ai​Bj,fi​j​k∈ℚ.F(A,B)_{k}=\sum_{i,j}f_{ijk}A_{i}B_{j},\qquad f_{ijk}\in\mathbb{Q}. (1)

The same formula defines the map on scalars and on compatible matrix coefficients. In particular, it commutes with concatenating or splitting column blocks of BB. The numbers fi​j​kf_{ijk} are its coefficient array. Each map includes its input spaces and output space in its specification.

We write [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}, use natural logarithms, and allow constants in Oc​(⋅)O_{c}(\cdot) to depend on cc. An explicit construction is a finite algorithm producing its parameters and rational linear maps.

2.1 Packing and composition

A packing computes prescribed target maps using linear encodings, a list of source maps, and linear decoding. Keeping the two input encodings separate will allow transposition and substitution of matrix blocks.

Definition 2.1 (Packing).

Let TT and S1,…,SαS_{1},\ldots,S_{\alpha} be bilinear maps on specified finite-dimensional spaces. A packing of TT using these sources consists of linear encoders Ej,HjE_{j},H_{j} into the input spaces of SjS_{j} and linear decoders DjD_{j} from the output space of SjS_{j} to that of TT, satisfying

∑j=1αDj​(Sj​(Ej​(X),Hj​(Y)))=T⁡(X,Y)\sum_{j=1}^{\alpha}D_{j}\!\left(S_{j}(E_{j}(X),H_{j}(Y))\right)=T(X,Y) (2)

for all inputs (X,Y)(X,Y) of TT. It is same-left if every EjE_{j} is the identity. A packing modulo ε\varepsilon allows coefficients in ℚ⁡[ε,ε−1]\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}] in the linear maps and replaces (2) by Zε=T+ε​RεZ_{\varepsilon}=T+\varepsilon R_{\varepsilon}, where ZεZ_{\varepsilon} is the decoded map and RεR_{\varepsilon} is bilinear with coefficients in ℚ⁡[ε]\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon].

We write D⁡(W1,…,Wα)=∑j=1αDj​(Wj)D(W_{1},\ldots,W_{\alpha})=\sum_{j=1}^{\alpha}D_{j}(W_{j}) for the combined decoder. For a list of independent targets, take T⁡(𝐀,𝐁)=(Ti​(Ai,Bi))iT(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})=(T_{i}(A_{i},B_{i}))_{i}; for a same-left list, take T⁡(A,𝐁)=(Ti​(A,Bi))iT(A,\mathbf{B})=(T_{i}(A,B_{i}))_{i}. If all sources equal SS, we say that the packing uses α\alpha copies of SS. Packings of polynomial products or their coefficient windows are polynomial packings (PP); SL-PP denotes the same-left case. The parameter ε\varepsilon is distinct from the polynomial variables.

We recall two standard closure properties of bilinear algorithms: composition and combination on separate indices; see [BCS97, Chapters 14–15]. We give proofs in our notation for completeness.

When replacing a source computation by a packing, we use a sufficiently high power of ε\varepsilon in the replacement to preserve correctness modulo ε\varepsilon.

Lemma 2.2 (Composition).

Suppose TT has a packing modulo ε\varepsilon using S1,…,SαS_{1},\ldots,S_{\alpha}, and each SjS_{j} has a packing modulo ε\varepsilon using Rj,1,…,Rj,βjR_{j,1},\ldots,R_{j,\beta_{j}}. For a computable positive integer KK, replacing each source SjS_{j} by its packing with ε\varepsilon replaced by εK\varepsilon^{K} gives a packing of TT modulo ε\varepsilon using (Rj,k)j,k(R_{j,k})_{j,k}.

Proof.

Choose nonnegative integers pE,pH,pDp_{E},p_{H},p_{D} so that the powers of ε\varepsilon in the coefficients of the left encoders, right encoders, and decoders of the packing of TT have exponents at least −pE,−pH,−pD-p_{E},-p_{H},-p_{D}, respectively. Choose K=pE+pH+pD+1K=p_{E}+p_{H}+p_{D}+1. Each replacement has decoded error divisible by εK\varepsilon^{K}. Bilinearity shows that applying the outer encoders and decoders can lower its exponent by at most pE+pH+pDp_{E}+p_{H}+p_{D}, so every added error remains divisible by ε\varepsilon. The original decoded map is already congruent to TT modulo ε\varepsilon, and the composite encoders and decoders are linear. ∎

We also combine computations on separate coefficient indices. For maps F,GF,G with coefficient arrays f,gf,g, their tensor product is the bilinear map defined by (F⊗G)​(X,Y)k,k′=∑i,j,i′,j′fi​j​k​gi′​j′​k′​Xi,i′​Yj,j′(F\otimes G)(X,Y)_{k,k^{\prime}}=\sum_{i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}f_{ijk}g_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}k^{\prime}}X_{i,i^{\prime}}Y_{j,j^{\prime}}.

Lemma 2.3 (Combining separate indices).

If FF has a packing using S1,…,SαS_{1},\ldots,S_{\alpha} and GG has a packing using R1,…,RβR_{1},\ldots,R_{\beta}, then F⊗GF\otimes G has a packing using (Sj⊗Rk)j,k(S_{j}\otimes R_{k})_{j,k}, obtained by encoding along the two indices and decoding in reverse order. The conclusion holds also modulo the same parameter ε\varepsilon.

Proof.

Abbreviating each list of sources, the correctness identities are

D⁡(S⁡(E⁡(X),H⁡(Y)))=F⁡(X,Y),D′​(R⁡(E′​(X),H′​(Y)))=G⁡(X,Y).D(S(E(X),H(Y)))=F(X,Y),\qquad D^{\prime}(R(E^{\prime}(X),H^{\prime}(Y)))=G(X,Y).

Expand the combined computation and group its sums by the unprimed indices. The primed encoding, computation, and decoding form the second identity; substitute it. Applying the first identity to each remaining term gives coefficient fi​j​k​gi′​j′​k′f_{ijk}g_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}k^{\prime}}. This uses only finite sums and linearity of the encoders and decoders. Modulo ε\varepsilon, make the same substitutions with the complete decoded maps: their polynomial coefficient arrays multiply, and their constant coefficients are ff and gg. ∎

In particular, combining matrix multiplications of dimensions (p,q,r)(p,q,r) and (p′,q′,r′)(p^{\prime},q^{\prime},r^{\prime}) gives dimensions (p​p′,q​q′,r​r′)(pp^{\prime},qq^{\prime},rr^{\prime}): the row, inner, and column indices are respectively paired. Appendix A gives the other operation we use, exchanging the input and output roles of a packing.

2.2 The primal and dual gadgets

Our first packing extends the three-for-one gadget of [Ope26a, Lemma 4.2]. It computes c+1c+1 full products and one middle product from cc full products, allowing tt additional coefficients in each source right input. For t=1t=1, this adds just one coefficient; larger tt permits smaller cc.

Throughout the polynomial constructions, write s=a+b−1s=a+b-1 and define

Fulla,b⁡(A,B)=A​B,Mida,b⁡(A,Q)=([za−1+j]​(A​Q))j=0b−1,\operatorname{Full}_{a,b}(A,B)=AB,\qquad\operatorname{Mid}_{a,b}(A,Q)=\bigl([z^{a-1+j}](AQ)\bigr)_{j=0}^{b-1},

where the lengths of A,B,QA,B,Q are a,b,sa,b,s, respectively. Full returns ss coefficients, and Mid returns the bb coefficients at exponents a−1,…,s−1a-1,\ldots,s-1.

Lemma 2.4 (Primal packing).

For positive integers a,b,c,ta,b,c,t with c​t≥a+2​b−1ct\geq a+2b-1, there is a same-left packing modulo ε\varepsilon of

((Fulla,b⁡(A,Pi))i=1c+1,Mida,b⁡(A,Q))\bigl((\operatorname{Full}_{a,b}(A,P_{i}))_{i=1}^{c+1},\operatorname{Mid}_{a,b}(A,Q)\bigr)

using cc copies of Fulla,b+t\operatorname{Full}_{a,b+t}. Target and source coefficient sizes are p×q,q×rp\times q,q\times r for arbitrary positive integers p,q,rp,q,r.

Proof.

We are given AA of length aa, polynomials P1,…,Pc+1P_{1},\ldots,P_{c+1} of length bb, and QQ of length ss. We will encode only the right inputs, multiply the encoded polynomials by the unchanged AA, and recover the requested coefficients from these products.

Encoding procedure.

Since c​t≥s+b>sct\geq s+b>s, we can split the coefficient list of QQ into cc consecutive blocks of length tt, padding with zeros:

Q(j)​(z)=∑v=0t−1[zt⁡(j−1)+v]​Q​zv,Q⁡(z)=∑j=1czt⁡(j−1)​Q(j)​(z).Q^{(j)}(z)=\sum_{v=0}^{t-1}[z^{t(j-1)+v}]Q\,z^{v},\qquad Q(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{c}z^{t(j-1)}Q^{(j)}(z).

For 1≤j≤c1\leq j\leq c, set

Ej=Pj−zt​Pj+1+ε​zb​Q(j).E_{j}=P_{j}-z^{t}P_{j+1}+\varepsilon z^{b}Q^{(j)}.

The first two terms combine adjacent right inputs using a shift of tt. The last term places one block of ε​Q\varepsilon Q in positions b,…,b+t−1b,\ldots,b+t-1. All three terms have degree less than b+tb+t, so each EjE_{j} is a valid right input to Fulla,b+t\operatorname{Full}_{a,b+t}.

Compute the cc full source products Wj=A​EjW_{j}=AE_{j}, each of length s+ts+t.

Decoding procedure.

From these products, form the following telescoping sum:

W\displaystyle W =∑j=1czt⁡(j−1)​Wj\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{c}z^{t(j-1)}W_{j} (3)
=∑j=1czt⁡(j−1)​A​Pj−∑j=1czt​j​A​Pj+1+ε​zb​A​∑j=1czt⁡(j−1)​Q(j)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{c}z^{t(j-1)}AP_{j}-\sum_{j=1}^{c}z^{tj}AP_{j+1}+\varepsilon z^{b}A\sum_{j=1}^{c}z^{t(j-1)}Q^{(j)}
=A​P1+ε​zb​A​Q−zc​t​A​Pc+1.\displaystyle=AP_{1}+\varepsilon z^{b}AQ-z^{ct}AP_{c+1}.

In coefficient notation, this means computing

[zk]​W=∑j=1c[zk−t⁡(j−1)]​Wj,[z^{k}]W=\sum_{j=1}^{c}[z^{k-t(j-1)}]W_{j},

so forming WW is a fixed linear operation on the source outputs. For each 2≤j≤c2\leq j\leq c, the term zt⁡(j−1)​A​Pjz^{t(j-1)}AP_{j} occurs once with each sign and cancels. Only the two endpoint products remain, while the blocks of QQ reassemble into QQ.

Recover the middle product.

The first endpoint product A​P1AP_{1} has no coefficients at exponents ss or above. The last endpoint product zc​t​A​Pc+1z^{ct}AP_{c+1} has no coefficients below c​t≥s+bct\geq s+b. Thus neither contributes at exponents s,…,s+b−1s,\ldots,s+b-1. For 0≤k<b0\leq k<b, we obtain

ε−1​[zs+k]​W=[zs+k−b]​(A​Q)=[za−1+k]​(A​Q).\varepsilon^{-1}[z^{s+k}]W=[z^{s+k-b}](AQ)=[z^{a-1+k}](AQ).

These are exactly the bb coefficients of Mida,b⁡(A,Q)\operatorname{Mid}_{a,b}(A,Q). The division by ε\varepsilon is exact: every extracted coefficient has a factor ε\varepsilon, and the resulting output is independent of ε\varepsilon.

Recover the full products.

First take the first ss coefficients of WW:

Z1=∑k=0s−1[zk]​W​zk.Z_{1}=\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}[z^{k}]W\,z^{k}.

Equation (3) gives Z1≡A​P1(modε)Z_{1}\equiv AP_{1}\pmod{\varepsilon}: the final endpoint product does not reach this range, and the contribution from QQ is divisible by ε\varepsilon.

Once ZjZ_{j} is known, subtract WjW_{j}, discard the first tt coefficients, and take the next ss coefficients. In formulas, define the length-ss polynomial Zj+1Z_{j+1} by

[zk]​Zj+1=[zk+t]​(Zj−Wj),0≤k<s,1≤j≤c.[z^{k}]Z_{j+1}=[z^{k+t}](Z_{j}-W_{j}),\qquad 0\leq k<s,\quad 1\leq j\leq c.

To verify this step, suppose Zj≡A​Pj(modε)Z_{j}\equiv AP_{j}\pmod{\varepsilon}. Then

Zj−Wj\displaystyle Z_{j}-W_{j} =Zj−A​Pj+zt​A​Pj+1−ε​zb​A​Q(j)\displaystyle=Z_{j}-AP_{j}+z^{t}AP_{j+1}-\varepsilon z^{b}AQ^{(j)}
≡zt​A​Pj+1(modε).\displaystyle\equiv z^{t}AP_{j+1}\pmod{\varepsilon}.

Reading coefficients t,…,t+s−1t,\ldots,t+s-1 therefore recovers every coefficient of A​Pj+1AP_{j+1} modulo ε\varepsilon. Induction yields Zj≡A​Pj(modε)Z_{j}\equiv AP_{j}\pmod{\varepsilon} for all 1≤j≤c+11\leq j\leq c+1.

The encoding is linear in the right inputs. Every decoding step is a shift, a sum, a coefficient extraction, or multiplication by ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, so the combined decoder is linear in W1,…,WcW_{1},\ldots,W_{c}. All ZjZ_{j} are polynomial in ε\varepsilon, since their recovery uses no division by ε\varepsilon, and the middle output is exact. Hence the decoded map has no negative powers and equals the requested target modulo ε\varepsilon. The left input is unchanged, and the only products computed are the cc sources WjW_{j}. ∎

For c=1c=1 and t=a+2​b−1t=a+2b-1, this specializes to the three-for-one degeneration of [Ope26a, Lemma 4.2]. We next transpose the packing to reverse the counts: cc middle products will compute c+1c+1 middle products and one full product.

Lemma 2.5 (Dual packing).

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 2.4, there is a same-left packing modulo ε\varepsilon of

((Mida,b⁡(A,Qi))i=1c+1,Fulla,b⁡(A,P))\bigl((\operatorname{Mid}_{a,b}(A,Q_{i}))_{i=1}^{c+1},\operatorname{Full}_{a,b}(A,P)\bigr)

using cc copies of Mida,b+t\operatorname{Mid}_{a,b+t}, with the same coefficient sizes p×q,q×rp\times q,q\times r.

Proof.

Set A~​(z)=∑i=0a−1Ai𝖳​za−1−i\widetilde{A}(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}A_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}z^{a-1-i}. For a fixed AA, coefficient extraction gives, for every length λ\lambda,

Fulla,λ⁡(A~,⋅)𝖳=Mida,λ⁡(A,⋅),Mida,λ⁡(A~,⋅)𝖳=Fulla,λ⁡(A,⋅).\operatorname{Full}_{a,\lambda}(\widetilde{A},\cdot)^{\mathsf{T}}=\operatorname{Mid}_{a,\lambda}(A,\cdot),\qquad\operatorname{Mid}_{a,\lambda}(\widetilde{A},\cdot)^{\mathsf{T}}=\operatorname{Full}_{a,\lambda}(A,\cdot).

Here transpose is taken over all scalar entries of the coefficient lists. For example, the jjth coefficient of the first transpose is ∑iAi​Qa−1+j−i\sum_{i}A_{i}Q_{a-1+j-i}. Apply the primal packing to A~\widetilde{A} and transpose its map from the entire list of right inputs to the entire list of outputs. That target map is block diagonal, with c+1c+1 Full blocks and one Mid block. The displayed identities exchange each block and each source, for λ=b\lambda=b and b+tb+t. Lemma A.1 swaps the encoder and decoder by transposition and preserves correctness modulo ε\varepsilon. ∎

2.3 Packing across variables

We now combine the two gadgets to amplify their gain. We first allow the positions of the full and middle ranges to depend on the target; the next subsection will put all targets into one common form.

Use 2​d2d variables z1,…,z2​dz_{1},\ldots,z_{2d}. For I⊆[2​d]I\subseteq[2d], let Fa,b,I​(A,B)F_{a,b,I}(A,B) compute the coefficients of A​BAB that are full in the variables indexed by II and middle in the others. Precisely, AA has length aa in every variable, BB has length bb on II and ss outside II, and the output consists of

([𝐳𝝂]​(A​B))νk∈{0,…,s−1}​(k∈I),νk∈{a−1,…,s−1}​(k∉I).\bigl([\mathbf{z}^{\boldsymbol{\nu}}](AB)\bigr)_{\nu_{k}\in\{0,\ldots,s-1\}\ (k\in I),\hskip 8.19447pt\nu_{k}\in\{a-1,\ldots,s-1\}\ (k\notin I)}.

Write I0=[d]I_{0}=[d] and Fa,b(d)=Fa,b,I0F_{a,b}^{(d)}=F_{a,b,I_{0}}. Thus Fa,b(d)F_{a,b}^{(d)} is full in the first dd variables and middle in the last dd.

We first count words with two types of letters. Different letters of the same type will represent different outputs of a packing.

Lemma 2.6 (Counting words by type).

For positive integers c,dc,d, let

𝒫={𝖥1,…,𝖥c+1,𝖬},𝒟={𝖥,𝖬1,…,𝖬c+1}.\mathcal{P}=\{\mathsf{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{F}_{c+1},\mathsf{M}\},\qquad\mathcal{D}=\{\mathsf{F},\mathsf{M}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{M}_{c+1}\}.

The letters 𝖥,𝖥i\mathsf{F},\mathsf{F}_{i} have type Full, and the letters 𝖬,𝖬i\mathsf{M},\mathsf{M}_{i} have type Mid. The number of words whose first dd letters lie in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, whose last dd letters lie in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and which contain exactly dd letters of each type is

∑h=0d(dh)2​(c+1)2​(d−h)≥(c+2)2​dd+1.\sum_{h=0}^{d}\binom{d}{h}^{2}(c+1)^{2(d-h)}\geq\frac{(c+2)^{2d}}{d+1}.
Proof.

Fix the number hh of Mid letters in the first half. Choose their hh positions; each must contain 𝖬\mathsf{M}. Each remaining position can contain any of the c+1c+1 distinct letters 𝖥1,…,𝖥c+1\mathsf{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{F}_{c+1}. There are therefore (dh)​(c+1)d−h\binom{d}{h}(c+1)^{d-h} choices for the first half.

The first half contains d−hd-h Full letters, so the second half must contain exactly hh Full letters. Choose their positions and put 𝖥\mathsf{F} in each. Each remaining position can contain any of the c+1c+1 Mid letters, giving the same number of choices. The two halves can be chosen independently, so multiplying their counts and summing over hh gives the stated equality. Finally,

∑h=0d[(dh)​(c+1)d−h]2≥[∑h=0d(dh)​(c+1)d−h]2d+1=(c+2)2​dd+1\sum_{h=0}^{d}\left[\binom{d}{h}(c+1)^{d-h}\right]^{2}\geq\frac{\left[\sum_{h=0}^{d}\binom{d}{h}(c+1)^{d-h}\right]^{2}}{d+1}=\frac{(c+2)^{2d}}{d+1}

by Cauchy–Schwarz and the binomial theorem. ∎

Lemma 2.7 (Same-left multivariate packing).

For positive integers c,dc,d, set

u=c2​d,w=⌊(c+2)2​dd+1⌋.u=c^{2d},\qquad w=\left\lfloor\frac{(c+2)^{2d}}{d+1}\right\rfloor. (4)

We begin with a common left input AA and an entire array of right inputs. Encoding.

Compress this array one variable at a time, in the order z1,…,z2​dz_{1},\ldots,z_{2d}. For d=1d=1, write x=z1x=z_{1} and y=z2y=z_{2}. Write the inputs as Bi,j​(x,y)B_{i,j}(x,y), where ii labels a primal output and jj a dual output. Fix jj, and expand Bi,j​(x,y)=∑vBi,j,v​(x)​yvB_{i,j}(x,y)=\sum_{v}B_{i,j,v}(x)y^{v}. If the results are U1,j,v​(x),…,Uc,j,v​(x)U_{1,j,v}(x),\ldots,U_{c,j,v}(x), reassemble Ur,j​(x,y)=∑vUr,j,v​(x)​yvU_{r,j}(x,y)=\sum_{v}U_{r,j,v}(x)y^{v}. For more variables, use their monomials in place of yvy^{v} in this same operation. At step kk, denote the resulting list by 𝐁(k)\mathbf{B}^{(k)}, with 𝐁(0)\mathbf{B}^{(0)} the original array. [Dx​(Dy​(S⁡(A,Ey​(Ex​(𝐁)))))]i,j≡Fi,j​(A,Bi,j)(modε).\left[D_{x}\!\left(D_{y}\!\left(S\!\left(A,E_{y}(E_{x}(\mathbf{B}))\right)\right)\right)\right]_{i,j}\equiv F_{i,j}(A,B_{i,j})\pmod{\varepsilon}.

Each recovered output is indexed by one word. Its Full set II consists of the positions occupied by Full letters. Thus the outputs with |I|=d|I|=d correspond exactly to the words counted in Lemma 2.6, which gives at least (c+2)2​d/(d+1)(c+2)^{2d}/(d+1) such outputs. 2.4 Independent left inputs and a common target

We next give each target its own left input. We encode all left inputs in one univariate polynomial and each group of right inputs in its own univariate polynomial. The right inputs in group ii are encoded at the points i+ε​ji+\varepsilon j. At each of these points, the left polynomial evaluates to AiA_{i} modulo ε\varepsilon. This lets one interpolated product recover the entire group modulo ε\varepsilon. Each target right input has MM column blocks; we recover the M2M^{2} narrow output blocks using 2​M−12M-1 applications of the same-left packing.

Lemma 2.8 (Separating left inputs).

Let M,N,u,p,q,rM,N,u,p,q,r be positive integers with M≥2M\geq 2, and let F0,…,FM−1,SF_{0},\ldots,F_{M-1},S be maps of the form (1). Suppose a same-left packing modulo ε\varepsilon computes (Fi​(A,Bi))i=0M−1(F_{i}(A,B_{i}))_{i=0}^{M-1} on coefficient sizes p×q,q×rp\times q,q\times r using NN copies of SS on sizes p×q,q×u​rp\times q,q\times ur. Then a packing modulo ε\varepsilon computes (Fi​(Ai,Bi))i=0M−1(F_{i}(A_{i},B_{i}))_{i=0}^{M-1} on sizes p×q,q×M​rp\times q,q\times Mr using N⁡(2​M−1)N(2M-1) copies of SS on sizes p×q,q×u​rp\times q,q\times ur.33 3 The encoding at the points i+ε​ji+\varepsilon j in the proof was proposed by Codex after I prompted it to solve this separation problem using Reed–Muller decoding [Sud02, Section 2.2].

Given independent pairs Ai,BiA_{i},B_{i}, write

Bi=[Bi,0⋯Bi,M−1],B_{i}=[\,B_{i,0}\ \cdots\ B_{i,M-1}\,],

splitting every q×M​rq\times Mr coefficient matrix horizontally into MM blocks of size q×rq\times r. Since FiF_{i} applies the same coefficient formula to each column block,

Fi(Ai,Bi)=[Fi(Ai,Bi,0)⋯Fi(Ai,Bi,M−1)].F_{i}(A_{i},B_{i})=[\,F_{i}(A_{i},B_{i,0})\ \cdots\ F_{i}(A_{i},B_{i,M-1})\,].

Thus we must recover all MM output blocks in each group ii.

Encode. Interpolate one input-valued polynomial A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) of degree at most M−1M-1 with A⁡(i)=AiA(i)=A_{i}. For each group ii, interpolate a right-input-valued polynomial Ci​(v)C_{i}(v) of degree at most M−1M-1 with Ci​(j)=Bi,jC_{i}(j)=B_{i,j}, and define

Bi′​(ξ)=Ci​(ξ−iε).B_{i}^{\prime}(\xi)=C_{i}\!\left(\frac{\xi-i}{\varepsilon}\right).

The division by ε\varepsilon preserves the distinct right inputs as their interpolation points approach ii:

Bi′​(i+ε​j)=Ci​(j)=Bi,j(0≤j<M).B_{i}^{\prime}(i+\varepsilon j)=C_{i}(j)=B_{i,j}\qquad(0\leq j<M).

Meanwhile, AA is independent of ε\varepsilon, so A⁡(i+ε​j)≡Ai(modε)A(i+\varepsilon j)\equiv A_{i}\pmod{\varepsilon}. We substitute ξ=i+ε​j\xi=i+\varepsilon j before taking the constant term: the coefficients of Bi′B_{i}^{\prime} may contain negative powers of ε\varepsilon. The points i,i+ε,…,i+ε⁡(M−1)i,i+\varepsilon,\ldots,i+\varepsilon(M-1) are distinct over ℚ⁡(ε)\mathbb{Q}(\varepsilon). Since CiC_{i} has degree at most M−1M-1, the coefficients of Bi′B_{i}^{\prime} are Laurent polynomials in ε\varepsilon whose powers have exponents at least −(M−1)-(M-1). Both encodings are linear in their respective inputs.

Compute and interpolate. Consider the univariate polynomials

Pi​(ξ)=Fi​(A⁡(ξ),Bi′​(ξ)).P_{i}(\xi)=F_{i}(A(\xi),B_{i}^{\prime}(\xi)).

Bilinearity gives degree at most 2​M−22M-2 in ξ\xi. Replace the given packing’s parameter by εM\varepsilon^{M}. Its decoded error is then divisible by εM\varepsilon^{M} before substituting the inputs. The left input contains no negative powers of ε\varepsilon, and the powers in the right inputs have exponents at least −(M−1)-(M-1). Since the error is bilinear, after substitution it is still divisible by εM−(M−1)=ε\varepsilon^{M-(M-1)}=\varepsilon.

P~i​(ξ)=Pi​(ξ)+ε​Ri​(ξ,ε),\widetilde{P}_{i}(\xi)=P_{i}(\xi)+\varepsilon R_{i}(\xi,\varepsilon),

where RiR_{i} has polynomial coefficients in ξ,ε\xi,\varepsilon.

We apply this lemma after concatenating the same-left source products into one wider product. With independent left inputs, each target can then be put into the canonical Full set I0I_{0}.

Theorem 2.9 (Multivariate polynomial packing).

Let c,dc,d be positive integers, take u,wu,w from (4), and put α=2​w−1\alpha=2w-1. If w≥2w\geq 2, then for all positive integers a,b,ta,b,t with c​t≥a+2​b−1ct\geq a+2b-1, there is a packing modulo ε\varepsilon of ww independent copies of Fa,b(d)F_{a,b}^{(d)} on coefficient sizes p×q,q×w​rp\times q,q\times wr, using α\alpha copies of Fa,b+t(d)F_{a,b+t}^{(d)} on sizes p×q,q×u​rp\times q,q\times ur, for all positive integers p,q,rp,q,r.

Proof.

Take the Full sets IiI_{i} and same-left packing from Lemma 2.7. Its uu source right inputs can be concatenated horizontally: the resulting single source has column width u​rur, and its output splits into the original uu outputs. Apply Lemma 2.8 with M=wM=w, N=1N=1, and S=Fa,b+t(d)S=F_{a,b+t}^{(d)}. This gives independent targets Fa,b,IiF_{a,b,I_{i}} with the claimed sizes and source count.

For each ii, choose the variable permutation πi\pi_{i} sending the first dd positions to the elements of IiI_{i} in increasing order, and the remaining positions to its complement in increasing order. Given canonical inputs (Ai,Bi)(A_{i},B_{i}), encode (πi​Ai,πi​Bi)(\pi_{i}A_{i},\pi_{i}B_{i}) in target ii and undo πi\pi_{i} on its output. Renaming variables commutes with multiplication and sends exactly the input lengths and output ranges of Fa,b(d)F_{a,b}^{(d)} to those of Fa,b,IiF_{a,b,I_{i}}. Consequently the decoded result is Fa,b(d)​(Ai,Bi)F_{a,b}^{(d)}(A_{i},B_{i}). The variable permutations depend only on c,dc,d; their induced coefficient reindexings are linear. ∎

For the exponent bound, take c≥2c\geq 2 and d=c3d=c^{3}. Rounding in (4) loses at most a factor of two, so

(1+2/c)2​d2​(d+1)≤wu≤(1+2/c)2​dd+1,log⁡(w/u)=4​c2+O⁡(c).\frac{(1+2/c)^{2d}}{2(d+1)}\leq\frac{w}{u}\leq\frac{(1+2/c)^{2d}}{d+1},\qquad\log(w/u)=4c^{2}+O(c). (5)

In particular w>2​uw>2u: using log⁡(1+x)≥x/(1+x)\log(1+x)\geq x/(1+x), the logarithm of the lower bound is at least 2​c2−3​log⁡c−2​log⁡2>log⁡22c^{2}-3\log c-2\log 2>\log 2 for c≥2c\geq 2.

3 Reducing all matrix dimensions

We now turn the column reduction into a reduction in rows, inner dimension, and columns simultaneously. We also establish the a↔ba\leftrightarrow b symmetry and the terminal multiplication bound needed to compose these reductions.

3.1 Three roles

For a bilinear map FF, the maps F(12)F^{(12)} and F(13)F^{(13)} exchange its two input roles and its left-input/output roles, respectively, as defined in Appendix A. Define

F^=F⊗F(12)⊗F(13).\widehat{F}=F\otimes F^{(12)}\otimes F^{(13)}.

The three factors act on separate coefficient indices. This construction allows the three matrix dimensions to be reduced by the same factor.

Lemma 3.1 (Packing in all dimensions).

Let M,α,u,wM,\alpha,u,w be positive integers and let F,SF,S be maps of the form (1). Suppose a packing computes MM independent copies of FF on coefficient sizes p×q,q×w​rp\times q,q\times wr using α\alpha copies of SS on sizes p×q,q×u​rp\times q,q\times ur, with the same scalar formulas for all compatible matrix blocks. Then M3M^{3} copies of F^\widehat{F} on sizes

p​w×q​w,q​w×r​wpw\times qw,\quad qw\times rw

can be packed into α3\alpha^{3} copies of S^\widehat{S} on sizes p​u×q​u,q​u×r​upu\times qu,qu\times ru. The implication holds modulo ε\varepsilon as well.

Proof.

The given reduction changes the matrix-dimension triple (p,q,w​r)(p,q,wr) to (p,q,u​r)(p,q,ur). Its (12)(12) role exchange gives (p​w,q,r)⟶(p​u,q,r)(pw,q,r)\longrightarrow(pu,q,r), and its (13)(13) exchange gives (p,q​w,r)⟶(p,q​u,r)(p,qw,r)\longrightarrow(p,qu,r), by Lemma A.1. Combine the three packings on separate coefficient groups and on the column, row, and inner block indices, respectively. Lemma 2.3 multiplies their target and source counts and gives the claimed sizes, leaving the outer block dimensions p,q,rp,q,r unchanged. ∎

3.2 Symmetry and terminal evaluation

For the remainder of the proof let Ga,b=Fa,b(d)^G_{a,b}=\widehat{F_{a,b}^{(d)}}, with dd fixed. The preceding lemma and Theorem 2.9 give a packing of w3w^{3} copies of Ga,bG_{a,b} into α3\alpha^{3} copies of Ga,b+tG_{a,b+t}. We first show that exchanging a,ba,b lets us apply this packing to either length parameter.

Lemma 3.2 (Symmetry).

For all positive integers a,ba,b, exchanging aa and bb in Ga,bG_{a,b} amounts to fixed reorderings of the coefficients of its inputs and output; the coefficient-matrix sizes remain unchanged.

Proof.

Put s=a+b−1s=a+b-1. Reverse the output coefficient index in Full and Mid, carrying this reversal along when exchanging roles. The six groups defining Ga,bG_{a,b} then contain all six orders of the lengths (a,b,s)(a,b,s), each repeated dd times, with the common coefficient condition i+j+k=s−1i+j+k=s-1. Exchanging a,ba,b simply permutes these groups. Undoing the coefficient reversals gives the asserted reordering. ∎

We next bound the cost of finishing the polynomial computation with ordinary matrix multiplication.

Lemma 3.3 (Terminal evaluation).

We have G1,1​(A,B)=A​BG_{1,1}(A,B)=AB. For every positive integer LL, GL,LG_{L,L} can be computed exactly using O⁡(L6​d)O(L^{6d}) matrix multiplications of the original coefficient sizes.

Proof.

At a=b=1a=b=1, every coefficient list has length one, giving A​BAB.

For a=b=La=b=L, the product of two scalar length-LL polynomials has degree O⁡(L)O(L). Standard evaluation and interpolation [BCS97, Chapter 14] computes Full using O⁡(L)O(L) scalar products: evaluate at O⁡(L)O(L) distinct rational points, multiply the values, and interpolate. Exchanging the right-input and output roles and reversing the left coefficient list gives Mid. Further role exchanges preserve this product count. Combine these algorithms over the 6​d6d coefficient directions, then substitute matrix coefficients, using Lemma 2.3. The result uses O⁡(L6​d)O(L^{6d}) matrix products of the original sizes. ∎

4 A fixed matrix multiplication identity

We now compose the packing in both length parameters. Each round shrinks the coefficient matrices and increases the polynomial lengths; the terminal bound in Lemma 3.3 accounts for the cost of those longer polynomials.

4.1 Construction of the identity

The next theorem produces a single finite rational identity. Once its parameters have been fixed, ordinary block recursion will apply it to matrices of arbitrary size.

Theorem 4.1 (A fixed identity).

For every τ>9/4\tau>9/4, there are computable integers v,r≥2v,r\geq 2 with r<vτr<v^{\tau}, rational linear forms ℓν,mν\ell_{\nu},m_{\nu} on v×vv\times v matrices, and rational matrices Wν∈ℚv×vW_{\nu}\in\mathbb{Q}^{v\times v} such that

A​B=∑ν=1rℓν​(A)​mν​(B)​Wν(A,B∈ℚv×v).AB=\sum_{\nu=1}^{r}\ell_{\nu}(A)m_{\nu}(B)W_{\nu}\qquad(A,B\in\mathbb{Q}^{v\times v}). (6)
Proof.

Fix c≥2c\geq 2, to be chosen sufficiently large, and take d=c3d=c^{3}, u,wu,w from (4), and α=2​w−1\alpha=2w-1. Set

R=⌊w/u⌋2,ρ=1+3c−1.R=\lfloor w/u\rfloor^{2},\qquad\rho=1+\frac{3}{c-1}.

We have w>2​uw>2u, R≥4R\geq 4, and log⁡R=8​c2+O⁡(c)\log R=8c^{2}+O(c) by (5).

One round.

Given w3w^{3} products of GL,LG_{L,L} with square coefficient matrices of side w2​R​nw^{2}Rn, put

t=⌈3​L−1c−1⌉,L′=L+t≤ρ​L+1.t=\left\lceil\frac{3L-1}{c-1}\right\rceil,\qquad L^{\prime}=L+t\leq\rho L+1.

The condition c​t≥a+2​b−1ct\geq a+2b-1 holds both at (a,b)=(L,L)(a,b)=(L,L) and at (L′,L)(L^{\prime},L), since (c−1)​t≥3​L−1(c-1)t\geq 3L-1. Theorem 2.9 and Lemma 3.1 first reduce the w3w^{3} given products to α3\alpha^{3} products of GL,L′G_{L,L^{\prime}} at matrix side w​u​R​nwuRn. Use Lemma 3.2 to replace each by GL′,LG_{L^{\prime},L}, permuting its coefficient lists and undoing the output permutation when decoding.

Since α<2​w\alpha<2w, put these products into eight batches of w3w^{3}, padding with zero inputs. Apply the same packing to each batch. This gives at most 8​α3<64​w38\alpha^{3}<64w^{3} products of GL′,L′G_{L^{\prime},L^{\prime}} at matrix side u2​R​n≤w2​nu^{2}Rn\leq w^{2}n. Pad to side w2​nw^{2}n and to 64​w364w^{3} products. Lemma 2.2 composes the two steps modulo one parameter. Thus a round divides the matrix side by RR, multiplies the product count by at most 6464, and changes LL to at most ρ​L+1\rho L+1.

Iteration.

Start one matrix product of side vk=w2​Rkv_{k}=w^{2}R^{k} in a list of w3w^{3} products of G1,1G_{1,1}, with zero inputs in the other positions. After kk rounds there are at most w3​64kw^{3}64^{k} products of GLk,LkG_{L_{k},L_{k}} at matrix side w2w^{2}, where

L0=1,Lk≤ρk+ρk−1ρ−1=Oc​(ρk).L_{0}=1,\qquad L_{k}\leq\rho^{k}+\frac{\rho^{k}-1}{\rho-1}=O_{c}(\rho^{k}).

Finish each using Lemma 3.3, and compute the remaining fixed-size matrix products by the elementary algorithm. Repeated use of Lemma 2.2 gives a packing modulo ε\varepsilon for the original matrix product with at most

rk=Oc​((64​ρ6​d)k)r_{k}=O_{c}\!\left((64\rho^{6d})^{k}\right)

scalar products. Its exponent satisfies

log⁡(64​ρ6​d)log⁡R=18​c2+O⁡(c)8​c2+O⁡(c)=94+O⁡(1/c).\frac{\log(64\rho^{6d})}{\log R}=\frac{18c^{2}+O(c)}{8c^{2}+O(c)}=\frac{9}{4}+O(1/c).

Choose cc so that 64​ρ6​d<Rτ64\rho^{6d}<R^{\tau}, and then kk so that rk<vkτr_{k}<v_{k}^{\tau}. These choices are finite and effective.

Removing the formal parameter.

Since rk<vkτr_{k}<v_{k}^{\tau}, Bini’s approximate-to-exact lemma [Bin80], stated and proved for completeness as Lemma B.1, converts this packing into an exact rational identity (6) at a computable finite side vv, using r<vτr<v^{\tau} scalar products. All coefficients arise from the stated encodings, permutations, and rational interpolations. ∎

The choice d=c3d=c^{3} gives convergence 9/4+O⁡(1/c)9/4+O(1/c). One can instead take d=c2d=c^{2}: then log⁡R=8​c+O⁡(log⁡c)\log R=8c+O(\log c) and log⁡(64​ρ6​d)=18​c+O⁡(1)\log(64\rho^{6d})=18c+O(1), giving 9/4+O⁡(log⁡c/c)9/4+O(\log c/c). This uses 6​c26c^{2} rather than 6​c36c^{3} polynomial variables, at the cost of slower convergence.

4.2 Integer arithmetic

We finish by applying standard block recursion to the fixed identity, as in Strassen’s algorithm [Str69]. Its parameters and coefficients are constants once the requested exponent is fixed.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Choose the identity in Theorem 4.1 with τ=9/4+γ\tau=9/4+\gamma. This identity also holds for matrix blocks: expanding both sides gives the same coefficient for every ordered product of a left-input block and a right-input block. Clear the fixed denominators in the encoders and decoder to obtain integer linear maps whose decoded output is δ​A​B\delta AB for a fixed positive integer δ\delta.

For n=vjn=v^{j}, partition the input matrices into v×vv\times v blocks, encode, recursively multiply the rr encoded pairs, decode, and divide every output entry exactly by δ\delta. All operations outside the recursive products cost O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}), so

T⁡(n)≤r​T​(n/v)+O⁡(n2)=O⁡(nτ),T(n)\leq rT(n/v)+O(n^{2})=O(n^{\tau}),

since r<vτr<v^{\tau} and τ>2\tau>2. Padding to the next power of vv handles every positive integer nn. ∎

For BB-bit integer inputs, encoding adds only O⁡(1)O(1) bits per level. Products have at most twice the resulting input length, and decoding adds O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) bits over the remaining levels. All intermediate integers therefore have O⁡(B+log⁡n)O(B+\log n) bits. The bit cost is O⁡(n9/4+γ​𝖬​(B+log⁡n))O(n^{9/4+\gamma}\mathsf{M}(B+\log n)), where 𝖬⁡(b)\mathsf{M}(b) is the cost of multiplying bb-bit integers; multiplication and exact division by the fixed constants take linear time.

The main ideas behind the construction, analysis, and abstractions are my own; Codex was invaluable in exploring definitions and proof approaches and in formalizing my proof ideas and sketches. Most of the text has been written and revised with Codex through detailed prompts from me. Claude provided feedback on the manuscript and its presentation.

Appendix A Exchanging input and output roles

We recall transposition of bilinear algorithms in the form used here; see [BCS97, Chapter 14 and Section 13.3]. For scalar lists, write ⟨U,V⟩=∑iUi​Vi\langle U,V\rangle=\sum_{i}U_{i}V_{i}. For matrices or lists of matrices, the sum runs over all scalar entries. Number the left input, right input, and output as roles 1,2,31,2,3. Define T(12)​(Y,X)=T⁡(X,Y)T^{(12)}(Y,X)=T(X,Y) and define the other exchanges by

⟨T(23)​(X,Z),Y⟩=⟨T⁡(X,Y),Z⟩=⟨T(13)​(Z,Y),X⟩.\langle T^{(23)}(X,Z),Y\rangle=\langle T(X,Y),Z\rangle=\langle T^{(13)}(Z,Y),X\rangle.

For a map of the form (1), an exchange of coefficient roles means exchanging the corresponding scalar indices first, then extending the resulting formula to matrix coefficients. An exchange of an entire matrix computation also exchanges its matrix-entry indices.

Lemma A.1 (Transposition).

If T⁡(X,Y)=∑jDj​Sj​(Ej​X,Hj​Y)T(X,Y)=\sum_{j}D_{j}S_{j}(E_{j}X,H_{j}Y) is a packing, then

T(23)​(X,Z)\displaystyle T^{(23)}(X,Z) =∑jHj𝖳​Sj(23)​(Ej​X,Dj𝖳​Z),\displaystyle=\sum_{j}H_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}S_{j}^{(23)}(E_{j}X,D_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}Z),
T(13)​(Z,Y)\displaystyle T^{(13)}(Z,Y) =∑jEj𝖳​Sj(13)​(Dj𝖳​Z,Hj​Y),\displaystyle=\sum_{j}E_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}S_{j}^{(13)}(D_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}Z,H_{j}Y),
T(12)​(Y,X)\displaystyle T^{(12)}(Y,X) =∑jDj​Sj(12)​(Hj​Y,Ej​X).\displaystyle=\sum_{j}D_{j}S_{j}^{(12)}(H_{j}Y,E_{j}X).

The same assertions hold modulo ε\varepsilon.

Proof.

For fixed XX, write TX​(Y)=T​(X,Y)T_{X}(Y)=T(X,Y). Correctness is the linear-map identity TX=∑jDj​(Sj)Ej​X​HjT_{X}=\sum_{j}D_{j}(S_{j})_{E_{j}X}H_{j}. Transposing it gives the first formula. Fixing YY gives the second, and exchanging the inputs gives the third. Each operation permutes the decoded coefficient array, preserving polynomiality in ε\varepsilon and its constant coefficient. ∎

For ordinary matrix multiplication, the corresponding dimension changes follow directly from

(A​B)𝖳=B𝖳​A𝖳,⟨A​B,C⟩=⟨A,C​B𝖳⟩=⟨B,A𝖳​C⟩.(AB)^{\mathsf{T}}=B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\langle AB,C\rangle=\langle A,CB^{\mathsf{T}}\rangle=\langle B,A^{\mathsf{T}}C\rangle.

Thus the exchanges (12),(23),(13)(12),(23),(13) send the dimension triple (p,q,r)(p,q,r) to (r,q,p),(q,p,r),(p,r,q)(r,q,p),(q,p,r),(p,r,q), respectively, up to transposing the input or output matrices.

Appendix B Removing the formal parameter

We state Bini’s amplification and interpolation argument [Bin80] in our packing notation and give the proof for completeness. It converts a packing modulo ε\varepsilon into an exact identity while making the interpolation cost negligible in the exponent.

Lemma B.1 (Bini’s approximate-to-exact conversion [Bin80]).

Suppose matrix multiplication of side v≥2v\geq 2 has a packing modulo ε\varepsilon using rr scalar products, and the coefficients of its decoded map have degree at most DD in ε\varepsilon. For every positive integer hh, there is an exact rational identity for matrix multiplication of side vhv^{h} using at most (h​D+1)​rh(hD+1)r^{h} scalar products. Consequently, for every τ>logv⁡r\tau>\log_{v}r, there is such an identity at a finite side VV with fewer than VτV^{\tau} scalar products. The identity can be computed from the given packing.

Proof.

Combine hh copies of the packing on separate matrix indices, using the same parameter ε\varepsilon in every copy. Lemma 2.3 gives a packing modulo ε\varepsilon for matrix multiplication of side V=vhV=v^{h} using rhr^{h} scalar products.

By the definition of a packing modulo ε\varepsilon, the coefficients of the fully decoded map are polynomials with no negative powers, and their constant terms are the coefficients of matrix multiplication. Each coefficient of the combined decoded map is a product of hh such polynomials. Its degree is therefore at most h​DhD, and its constant term is the product of their constant terms. Thus the constant term of the combined decoded map is precisely matrix multiplication of side VV.

Evaluate the encoders and decoders at h​D+1hD+1 distinct nonzero rational values of ε\varepsilon, for example 1,…,h​D+11,\ldots,hD+1. The encoding and decoding coefficients are Laurent polynomials, so all these specializations are defined and rational. Polynomial interpolation expresses the constant coefficient of the decoded map as a fixed rational linear combination of its values at these points. Each evaluation uses rhr^{h} scalar products, giving an exact rational identity with at most (h​D+1)​rh(hD+1)r^{h} scalar products.

If τ>logv⁡r\tau>\log_{v}r, then

(h​D+1)​rh(vh)τ=(h​D+1)​(rvτ)h⟶0.\frac{(hD+1)r^{h}}{(v^{h})^{\tau}}=(hD+1)\left(\frac{r}{v^{\tau}}\right)^{h}\longrightarrow 0.

Choose a finite hh for which this ratio is less than one. All steps use finite combinations of the given coefficient maps and rational interpolation, so the resulting identity is computable. ∎
